terms.title: 180-Degree Rule
terms.subtitle: An invisible axis between two people or objects that must not be crossed. Breaking the rul...
terms.definition: An invisible axis between two people or objects that must not be crossed. Breaking the rule makes the cut disorienting.

terms.title: A-Roll
terms.subtitle: The main footage of a production — typically interviews or the central action. Contrasts w...
terms.definition: The main footage of a production — typically interviews or the central action. Contrasts with B-Roll, which serves as illustrative supplementary material.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: A-Roll is the backbone of your video. It contains the main story, dialogue, and interviews around which everything else is built. Without strong A-Roll, viewers lose track.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: A-Roll is like the frame of a house. B-Roll is the facade and furniture — beautiful, but without the frame, nothing stands.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: A-Roll determines whether your story is understood. Good editing of the A-Roll makes the difference between confusing and captivating.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: In a documentary, the expert interview is the A-Roll. Footage of their laboratory is the B-Roll.

terms.title: Aperture
terms.subtitle: The opening in the lens through which light passes onto the sensor. Expressed as f-stop (e...
terms.definition: The opening in the lens through which light passes onto the sensor. Expressed as f-stop (e.g., f/1.8, f/2.8, f/16). Wide aperture = shallow depth of field, lots of light. Small aperture = everything sharp, less light.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: The aperture is the iris-like opening in your lens. It controls how much light hits the sensor and how much of the image is in focus. A wide aperture (low f-number) lets in lots of light and creates a blurred background.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Think of aperture like the pupil of your eye. In darkness it widens (wide aperture), in bright light it narrows (small aperture).

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Aperture is the most powerful tool for image aesthetics. It decides whether your portrait looks professional or like a casual snapshot.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: For a portrait with a blurred background you choose f/1.8. For a landscape where everything should be sharp, you use f/11.

terms.title: Aspect Ratio
terms.subtitle: The ratio of image width to height, e.g. 16:9 (standard TV), 9:16 (social media stories), ...
terms.definition: The ratio of image width to height, e.g. 16:9 (standard TV), 9:16 (social media stories), 2.39:1 (cinema). Fundamentally shapes the visual experience.

terms.title: Audio Clipping
terms.subtitle: Distortion that occurs when audio is recorded too loud (over 0 dBFS). Not recoverable i...
terms.definition: Distortion that occurs when audio is recorded too loud (over 0 dBFS). Not recoverable in post. A limiter protects against clipping.

terms.title: Audio Levels
terms.subtitle: Volume of the audio recording, measured in dB (decibels). Optimal: speech at approx. -1...
terms.definition: Volume of the audio recording, measured in dB (decibels). Optimal: speech at approx. -12 dBFS, never over 0 dBFS (clipping/distortion). Headroom of 6–12 dB is standard.

terms.title: Autofocus (AF)
terms.subtitle: Automatic camera focusing. Modern AF systems detect faces, eyes, or objects and keep them ...
terms.definition: Automatic camera focusing. Modern AF systems detect faces, eyes, or objects and keep them sharp — essential for moving subjects.

terms.title: B-Roll
terms.subtitle: Supplementary footage that illustrates the main story: details, environments, reactions. G...
terms.definition: Supplementary footage that illustrates the main story: details, environments, reactions. Good B-Roll transforms a dry interview into a compelling video.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: B-Roll is all the supplementary footage that supports your main story. It shows details, environments, reactions, and prevents your video from looking like a PowerPoint.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: A-Roll is like the narrator of a story. B-Roll is the book's illustrations — it makes the story visible and tangible.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Without B-Roll, you're stuck on one image in the edit. With good B-Roll you can bridge jumps in the A-Roll and build tension.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: In an interview, the chef talks about their favorite recipe. B-Roll shows the chopping of ingredients and the sizzling meat in the pan.

terms.title: Bitrate
terms.subtitle: Amount of data per time unit in a video. Higher bitrate = better quality but larger file. ...
terms.definition: Amount of data per time unit in a video. Higher bitrate = better quality but larger file. Critical for stable streaming playback.

terms.title: Bokeh
terms.subtitle: The aesthetic quality of out-of-focus areas in an image. Beautiful bokeh has smooth, circu...
terms.definition: The aesthetic quality of out-of-focus areas in an image. Beautiful bokeh has smooth, circular light spots and creamy transitions — achieved with a wide aperture.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: Bokeh describes the aesthetic quality of the out-of-focus areas in your image. Good bokeh features smooth, circular light spots and creamy transitions.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Bokeh is like the background at a fancy restaurant — softly blurred, elegant, and never distracting from your dinner companion.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Beautiful bokeh separates your subject from messy backgrounds and adds a professional, cinematic feel that viewers instinctively respond to.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: At night, streetlights behind your subject turn into soft, glowing orbs with a good 50mm f/1.8 lens.

terms.title: Call Sheet
terms.subtitle: Daily shooting schedule: call times, locations, scenes, required equipment. The most im...
terms.definition: Daily shooting schedule: call times, locations, scenes, required equipment. The most important organizational document on set. Without a Call Sheet, chaos reigns.

terms.title: Close-Up
terms.subtitle: A shot that fills the frame with a face or detail. Creates intimacy, emotion, and directs ...
terms.definition: A shot that fills the frame with a face or detail. Creates intimacy, emotion, and directs attention precisely to what matters.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: A close-up fills the frame with a face or important detail. It eliminates distractions and forces the viewer to engage with the subject intimately.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: A close-up is like leaning in close to someone telling you a secret. Everything else disappears, and their expression becomes your entire world.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Close-ups carry emotion. A tear, a smile, or a twitching eye tells more than a thousand words in a wide shot.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: In an interview, cut to a close-up when the subject reveals something personal. The audience feels the intimacy of the moment.

terms.title: Codec
terms.subtitle: Method for compressing and decompressing video data. H.264 (web), H.265/HEVC (more efficie...
terms.definition: Method for compressing and decompressing video data. H.264 (web), H.265/HEVC (more efficient), ProRes (high quality, large files).

terms.title: Color Grading
terms.subtitle: Color adjustment in editing that defines the mood and look of a video. Differs from color ...
terms.definition: Color adjustment in editing that defines the mood and look of a video. Differs from color correction, which only aims for neutrality.

terms.title: Color Temperature
terms.subtitle: Measured in Kelvin (K): describes the color of a light source. Low (3200K) = warm/oran...
terms.definition: Measured in Kelvin (K): describes the color of a light source. Low (3200K) = warm/orange (candle, tungsten). High (5600K+) = cool/blue (daylight, overcast sky).

terms.title: Continuity
terms.subtitle: Consistency of details between consecutive shots: clothing, props, lighting, camera pos...
terms.definition: Consistency of details between consecutive shots: clothing, props, lighting, camera position. Continuity errors (e.g., disappearing glass) destroy immersion.

terms.title: Crop
terms.subtitle: Trimming an image to change the aspect ratio or reframe the shot. 4K footage can be croppe...
terms.definition: Trimming an image to change the aspect ratio or reframe the shot. 4K footage can be cropped to 1080p without quality loss, allowing reframing in post.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: Cropping means trimming the edges of your frame to recompose the shot or change aspect ratio. With high-resolution footage, you can crop significantly without quality loss.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Cropping is like using scissors on a photograph. You cut away what doesn't belong and focus attention on what matters.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Cropping in post saves shots that were framed poorly on set. It also lets you create multiple compositions from a single master shot.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: You film a wide shot in 4K and later crop a medium close-up for a different angle, giving the illusion of a second camera.

terms.title: Cross Dissolve
terms.subtitle: A soft transition where one image slowly fades out while the next fades in. Signals the pa...
terms.definition: A soft transition where one image slowly fades out while the next fades in. Signals the passage of time or a gentle change of location.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: A cross dissolve is a soft transition where one clip gradually fades out while the next fades in. It creates a gentle passage of time or location.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: A cross dissolve is like falling asleep and waking up in a new place. The world blurs for a moment, and when it clears, you're somewhere else.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Unlike a hard cut, a dissolve signals emotional or temporal distance. It softens transitions and can add poetry to your edit.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: You use a cross dissolve to show a character remembering their childhood — the present blurs into the past.

terms.title: Depth of Field
terms.subtitle: The range in which the image is sharp. Wide aperture (e.g. f/1.8) = shallow depth of field...
terms.definition: The range in which the image is sharp. Wide aperture (e.g. f/1.8) = shallow depth of field, blurred background. Small aperture = everything sharp.

terms.title: Diffusion
terms.subtitle: Softening light through a translucent material (softbox, diffusion gel, parchment paper...
terms.definition: Softening light through a translucent material (softbox, diffusion gel, parchment paper). Hard light creates hard shadows; soft light creates flowing shadows — essential for skin.

terms.title: Dolly
terms.subtitle: Camera movement on tracks or wheels toward or away from the subject. Creates dramatic spat...
terms.definition: Camera movement on tracks or wheels toward or away from the subject. Creates dramatic spatial depth and a professional feel.

terms.title: Dutch Angle
terms.subtitle: Tilted camera (not horizontal). Signals discomfort, confusion, or tension. Used sparingly ...
terms.definition: Tilted camera (not horizontal). Signals discomfort, confusion, or tension. Used sparingly for maximum impact.

terms.title: Dynamic Range
terms.subtitle: Span between the brightest and darkest detail a camera can capture simultaneously. High ...
terms.definition: Span between the brightest and darkest detail a camera can capture simultaneously. High Dynamic Range (12+ stops) preserves detail in shadows and highlights.

terms.title: Encoding
terms.subtitle: Conversion of raw material into a compressed format. Hardware encoding (GPU) is faster; so...
terms.definition: Conversion of raw material into a compressed format. Hardware encoding (GPU) is faster; software encoding (CPU) often yields better quality.

terms.title: Establishing Shot
terms.subtitle: A wide shot at the beginning of a scene that establishes location, time, and atmosphere. G...
terms.definition: A wide shot at the beginning of a scene that establishes location, time, and atmosphere. Gives the viewer spatial orientation before close-ups follow.

terms.title: Export
terms.subtitle: Rendering the finished video into a playable format. Key parameters: codec, resolution, fr...
terms.definition: Rendering the finished video into a playable format. Key parameters: codec, resolution, frame rate, bitrate, and color space.

terms.title: Exposure
terms.subtitle: Amount of light hitting the sensor. Determined by aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. Cor...
terms.definition: Amount of light hitting the sensor. Determined by aperture, shutter speed, and ISO. Correct exposure prevents over- or underexposure and preserves detail.

terms.title: Exposé
terms.subtitle: A short summary of a film idea: concept, target audience, style, budget outline. The expos...
terms.definition: A short summary of a film idea: concept, target audience, style, budget outline. The exposé convinces clients or funders before the script is written.

terms.title: Fade In / Fade Out
terms.subtitle: Slow fade of the image to/from black (or white). Fade In = beginning of a scene or film. F...
terms.definition: Slow fade of the image to/from black (or white). Fade In = beginning of a scene or film. Fade Out = ending. Classic, timeless, elegant.

terms.title: Focal Length
terms.subtitle: Distance between lens and sensor. Short focal length (wide angle, e.g. 18mm) = lots in fra...
terms.definition: Distance between lens and sensor. Short focal length (wide angle, e.g. 18mm) = lots in frame, perspective distortion. Long focal length (tele, e.g. 85mm) = flat background, compressed perspective.

terms.title: Foley
terms.subtitle: The art of recreating sounds in post: footsteps, doors, clothing. Foley artists work with ...
terms.definition: The art of recreating sounds in post: footsteps, doors, clothing. Foley artists work with everyday objects to create realistic sound worlds.

terms.title: Frame Grab
terms.subtitle: Extracting a single high-quality still image from a video. 4K video can produce 8-megapixe...
terms.definition: Extracting a single high-quality still image from a video. 4K video can produce 8-megapixel photos — useful for thumbnails or promotional images.

terms.title: Frame Rate
terms.subtitle: Number of frames per second. 24 fps = cinematic look, 25/30 fps = broadcast standard, 6...
terms.definition: Number of frames per second. 24 fps = cinematic look, 25/30 fps = broadcast standard, 60+ fps = smooth motion, 120+ fps = slow-motion footage.

terms.title: Frame Rate (FPS)
terms.subtitle: Number of frames per second. 24 fps = cinematic look, 25/30 fps = TV standard, 60+ fps = s...
terms.definition: Number of frames per second. 24 fps = cinematic look, 25/30 fps = TV standard, 60+ fps = smooth motion, 120+ fps = slow-motion material.

terms.title: Framing
terms.subtitle: The deliberate enclosing of the subject in the image. Doors, windows, branches, or arch...
terms.definition: The deliberate enclosing of the subject in the image. Doors, windows, branches, or architecture can serve as a natural frame, giving the image depth and context.

terms.title: Gain
terms.subtitle: Electronic amplification of the signal. Similar to ISO but used in video camcorders. High ...
terms.definition: Electronic amplification of the signal. Similar to ISO but used in video camcorders. High gain leads to digital noise.

terms.title: Gimbal
terms.subtitle: Motorized stabilizer for the camera. Compensates for movement in real time and enables but...
terms.definition: Motorized stabilizer for the camera. Compensates for movement in real time and enables buttery-smooth tracking shots without expensive equipment.

terms.title: Golden Hour
terms.subtitle: The period shortly after sunrise or before sunset with warm, soft light. The most importan...
terms.definition: The period shortly after sunrise or before sunset with warm, soft light. The most important time for atmospheric outdoor shots.

terms.title: HDR
terms.subtitle: High Dynamic Range — extended contrast and color space. HDR video shows more detail in bri...
terms.definition: High Dynamic Range — extended contrast and color space. HDR video shows more detail in bright and dark areas simultaneously. Requires compatible displays.

terms.title: Headroom
terms.subtitle: Empty space above a subject's head in the frame. Too little = decapitated head, too muc...
terms.definition: Empty space above a subject's head in the frame. Too little = decapitated head. Too much = subject floats in the frame. Optimal: about one head-height of space.

terms.title: Histogram
terms.subtitle: Graphical representation of brightness distribution in the image. Helps with correct expos...
terms.definition: Graphical representation of brightness distribution in the image. Helps with correct exposure — prevents highlights from clipping or shadows from crushing.

terms.title: Interlaced (i)
terms.subtitle: Legacy format where each frame consists of two fields (e.g. 1080i). Modern production uses...
terms.definition: Legacy format where each frame consists of two fields (e.g. 1080i). Modern production uses Progressive (p) for sharper motion.

terms.title: ISO
terms.subtitle: Sensor sensitivity to light. Low ISO (100–400) = clean image in good light. High ISO (1600...
terms.definition: Sensor sensitivity to light. Low ISO (100–400) = clean image in good light. High ISO (1600+) = more noise, needed in darkness.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: ISO determines the sensor's sensitivity to light. Low ISO (100–400) gives clean images in good light. High ISO (1600+) amplifies the signal and creates digital noise.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: ISO is like the volume on a music box. At low volume you hear only the music (clean image). At full volume you hear the amplifier hiss (digital noise).

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Noise is hard to remove and destroys the professionalism of your video. Better to use more light or open the aperture before raising ISO.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: In daylight outdoors, work at ISO 100–400. In a dimly lit conference room, you must go to ISO 1600–3200 — with visible noise as a compromise.

terms.title: J-Cut
terms.subtitle: The sound of the next clip begins before the image changes. Creates a smooth transition an...
terms.definition: The sound of the next clip begins before the image changes. Creates a smooth transition and draws the viewer into the next scene.

terms.title: Jump Cut
terms.subtitle: A cut within a single shot where portions of time are removed. Can be intentional for ener...
terms.definition: A cut within a single shot where portions of time are removed. Can be intentional for energy (vlogs) or unintentional as a mistake.

terms.title: Keying (Chroma Key)
terms.subtitle: Removing a color (usually green or blue) from the image to insert a new background. The fo...
terms.definition: Removing a color (usually green or blue) from the image to insert a new background. The foundation of green-screen effects.

terms.title: Keyframe
terms.subtitle: A marker point on the timeline that defines a specific state (e.g. position, size, color)....
terms.definition: A marker point on the timeline that defines a specific state (e.g. position, size, color). Values between keyframes are animated through interpolation.

terms.title: L-Cut
terms.subtitle: The image changes while the sound of the previous clip continues. A natural transition tha...
terms.definition: The image changes while the sound of the previous clip continues. A natural transition that maintains auditory continuity while moving the story forward.

terms.title: Lavalier (Lapel Mic)
terms.subtitle: Small microphone clipped to the speaker's shirt or jacket. Standard for interviews and ...
terms.definition: Small microphone clipped to the speaker's shirt or jacket. Standard for interviews and presentations. Delivers consistent, clear audio independent of head movement.

terms.title: Leading Lines
terms.subtitle: Lines in the image (paths, railings, building edges) that guide the viewer's eye toward...
terms.definition: Lines in the image (paths, railings, building edges, river courses) that guide the viewer's eye deliberately toward the subject. One of the strongest composition tools.

terms.title: Light
terms.subtitle: The fundamental element of every video production. Without light, there is no image. G...
terms.definition: The fundamental element of every video production. Without light, there is no image. Good light makes a consumer camera look professional.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: Light is the fundamental element of every video production. Without light, there is no image. The quality of your light matters more than any camera setting. Good light makes a consumer camera look professional.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Light is like paint for a painter. The best brush technique (camera) is useless if the paint is bad. Conversely, a good painter can create something beautiful even with simple paint.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: An average lighting setup is the fastest path to a professional look. Three-point lighting (Key, Fill, Backlight) is the standard every videographer must master.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: For an interview, place the Key Light at a 45° angle to the side, the Fill Light on the opposite side (half intensity), and a Backlight behind the subject to separate them from the background.

terms.title: Log Profile
terms.subtitle: Flat color profile that preserves maximum dynamic range and detail in highlights/shadow...
terms.definition: Flat color profile that preserves maximum dynamic range and detail in highlights/shadows. Requires color grading in post, but delivers the best source material.

terms.title: Lower Third
terms.subtitle: Graphic overlay in the lower part of the frame: name, title, role of a person. Often anima...
terms.definition: Graphic overlay in the lower part of the frame: name, title, role of a person. Often animated, with logo or color accent. Standard in documentaries and interviews.

terms.title: LUT
terms.subtitle: Look-Up Table — a color preset that remaps pixel values. Technical LUTs normalize log foot...
terms.definition: Look-Up Table — a color preset that remaps pixel values. Technical LUTs normalize log footage; creative LUTs give the video a specific look.

terms.title: Match Cut
terms.subtitle: Cut where shape, color, or motion of two consecutive shots match. An elegant transition...
terms.definition: Cut where shape, color, or motion of two consecutive shots match. An elegant transition tool that connects story and aesthetics.

terms.title: Medium Shot
terms.subtitle: A medium-close framing showing a person from the waist up. The most universal shot — conve...
terms.definition: A medium-close framing showing a person from the waist up. The most universal shot — conveys both emotion and body language.

terms.title: Montage
terms.subtitle: Assembling individual shots into a coherent whole. Good editing tells a story; bad editing...
terms.definition: Assembling individual shots into a coherent whole. Good editing tells a story; bad editing confuses the viewer.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: Editing is assembling clips into a story. There are different techniques: Hard Cut (direct), L-Cut (sound stays, picture changes), J-Cut (picture stays, sound changes). Good editing is invisible.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Editing is like writing a text. Individual words (clips) are available — editing puts them together into sentences, paragraphs, and stories.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: The best cut is the one the viewer doesn't notice. Bad editing destroys the story, no matter how good the footage is. Rhythm and timing are everything.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: In an interview, use J-Cuts: The audio of the next answer begins while B-Roll from the previous topic is still running. This creates smooth transitions without visible cuts.

terms.title: Motion Blur
terms.subtitle: Natural blur during fast movements due to longer shutter speed. Gives motion fluidity and ...
terms.definition: Natural blur during fast movements due to longer shutter speed. Gives motion fluidity and authenticity. Missing with too-fast shutter speeds.

terms.title: Narrative
terms.subtitle: The story a video tells. A clear narrative structure (beginning, conflict, resolution) kee...
terms.definition: The story a video tells. A clear narrative structure (beginning, conflict, resolution) keeps the viewer engaged until the end.

terms.title: ND Filter
terms.subtitle: Neutral density filter that reduces light without changing color. Enables wide apert...
terms.definition: Neutral density filter that reduces light without changing color. Enables wide apertures (e.g., f/1.8) in bright environments for shallow depth of field.

terms.title: Noise
terms.subtitle: Digital grain, especially in dark image areas. Caused by high ISO or low light. Good light...
terms.definition: Digital grain, especially in dark image areas. Caused by high ISO or low light. Good lighting is the best noise killer.

terms.title: Overexposure
terms.subtitle: Too much light on the sensor. Bright areas lose all detail and appear white ("clipping"). ...
terms.definition: Too much light on the sensor. Bright areas lose all detail and appear white ("clipping"). Harder to correct than underexposure.

terms.title: Over-the-Shoulder (OTS)
terms.subtitle: Camera angle over a person's shoulder looking at a subject. Standard for dialogues and int...
terms.definition: Camera angle over a person's shoulder looking at a subject. Standard for dialogues and interviews for spatial orientation.

terms.title: Pacing
terms.subtitle: Tempo and rhythm of the editing sequence. Fast cuts = energy, tension. Long shots = ca...
terms.definition: Tempo and rhythm of the editing sequence. Fast cuts = energy, tension. Long shots = calm, contemplation. Good pacing follows the emotional curve of the story.

terms.title: Pan
terms.subtitle: Horizontal camera movement left to right (or vice versa). Shows landscapes or follows move...
terms.definition: Horizontal camera movement left to right (or vice versa). Shows landscapes or follows movement. Should be slow and steady.

terms.title: Post-Production
terms.subtitle: All work after filming: editing, color grading, sound design, export. Can take more time t...
terms.definition: All work after filming: editing, color grading, sound design, export. Can take more time than the shoot itself.

terms.title: Proxy
terms.subtitle: Low-resolution copy of the original footage generated by the computer. Enables smooth e...
terms.definition: Low-resolution copy of the original footage generated by the computer. Enables smooth editing even on slower machines. Export automatically uses the original footage.

terms.title: Rack Focus
terms.subtitle: Deliberate focus shift from one object to another within a single shot. Subtly directs the...
terms.definition: Deliberate focus shift from one object to another within a single shot. Subtly directs the viewer's attention to the important detail.

terms.title: Reflector
terms.subtitle: Portable reflective surface that bounces existing light back onto the subject. The chea...
terms.definition: Portable reflective surface that bounces existing light back onto the subject. The cheapest and most versatile lighting tool — from a foldable reflector to simple cardboard.

terms.title: Render
terms.subtitle: The process of calculating the finished video from all tracks, effects, and settings. The ...
terms.definition: The process of calculating the finished video from all tracks, effects, and settings. The more complex the project, the longer the rendering.

terms.title: Resolution
terms.subtitle: The number of pixels making up an image. 1080p = 1920×1080, 4K = 3840×2160. Higher resolut...
terms.definition: The number of pixels making up an image. 1080p = 1920×1080, 4K = 3840×2160. Higher resolution means more detail but also larger files.

terms.title: Room Tone
terms.subtitle: Recording of the 'silence' of a room — no speaker, no movement. Essential for smooth c...
terms.definition: Recording of the 'silence' of a room — no speaker, no movement. Essential for smooth cuts, as every room has its own acoustic signature.

terms.title: Rule of Thirds
terms.subtitle: Composition rule: divide the image into a 3×3 grid, place important elements on the inters...
terms.definition: Composition rule: divide the image into a 3×3 grid, place important elements on the intersection points. Creates visual tension and aesthetics.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: The Rule of Thirds divides the image into a 3×3 grid. Important elements are placed on the intersections or lines — never in the dead center. This creates visual tension and a harmonious image.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: The Rule of Thirds is like hanging a picture. A picture in the center of the wall looks boring. Slightly offset, it feels more lively and interesting.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Our eyes are automatically drawn to the intersections. By placing the most important image elements there, you guide the viewer deliberately through your image.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: For a portrait, place one eye on the upper left intersection. For a landscape, the horizon lies on the lower or upper third line — never in the middle.

terms.title: Screenplay
terms.subtitle: The written foundation of a film: dialogues, action, camera directions, scene descriptions...
terms.definition: The written foundation of a film: dialogues, action, camera directions, scene descriptions. A good screenplay is half the work of any production.

terms.title: Shot List
terms.subtitle: Detailed list of all planned camera setups per scene: size, movement, lens, notes. The sho...
terms.definition: Detailed list of all planned camera setups per scene: size, movement, lens, notes. The shot list is the camera operator's shooting plan.

terms.title: Shutter Speed
terms.subtitle: The time the sensor receives light. Rule: shutter speed = 2× frame rate (e.g. 1/50s at 25 ...
terms.definition: The time the sensor receives light. Rule: shutter speed = 2× frame rate (e.g. 1/50s at 25 fps). Shorter = sharp motion; longer = motion blur.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: Shutter speed determines how long the sensor receives light. The 180° rule states: Shutter speed = 2 × frame rate (e.g., 1/50s at 25 fps). This creates natural motion blur, perceived like the human eye.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: Shutter speed is like blinking. A fast blink (short shutter speed) freezes motion. A slow blink (long shutter speed) lets motion blur.

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Too short a shutter speed (e.g., 1/1000s) makes motion stuttery and unnatural — the so-called 'Saving Private Ryan' effect. Too long a shutter speed creates excessive motion blur.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: For a cinematic look at 25 fps, set 1/50s. For sports action with sharp motion, use 1/100s. For dramatic slow motion at 120 fps, stay at 1/250s (180° rule).

terms.title: Slow Motion
terms.subtitle: Playback with fewer FPS than recorded. 120 fps at 24 fps = 5× slow motion. Captures detail...
terms.definition: Playback with fewer FPS than recorded. 120 fps at 24 fps = 5× slow motion. Captures details the eye normally doesn't see.

terms.title: Stinger / Intro
terms.subtitle: Short animation or sequence at the beginning (intro) or end (stinger/outro) of a video. St...
terms.definition: Short animation or sequence at the beginning (intro) or end (stinger/outro) of a video. Strengthens brand or channel recognition.

terms.title: Storyboard
terms.subtitle: Visual script draft: sketches of all scenes in order. Saves time on set and helps the enti...
terms.definition: Visual script draft: sketches of all scenes in order. Saves time on set and helps the entire team understand the vision.

terms.definition: Camera looks down on the subject from above. The subject appears small, vulnerable, or manageable. Often achieved with drones.

terms.title: White Balance
terms.subtitle: Setting that ensures white actually looks white — regardless of the light source (daylight...
terms.definition: Setting that ensures white actually looks white — regardless of the light source (daylight, incandescent, fluorescent). Prevents color casts.

blocks.heading: What does this mean?
blocks.content: White Balance tells the camera what 'true white' looks like depending on the light source (sun, tungsten bulb, fluorescent tube, LED). Measured in Kelvin: Daylight approx. 5600K, candlelight approx. 3200K.

blocks.heading: The Analogy
blocks.content: White Balance is like color-correction glasses for your camera. Without them, everything looks through a tinted lens — everything appears too warm (orange) or too cool (blue).

blocks.heading: Why does this matter?
blocks.content: Incorrect white balance makes skin tones look sick or unnatural. A deliberately wrong white balance can create mood — but it must be intentional.

blocks.heading: Example from practice
blocks.content: In an office with fluorescent tubes, set 4000K. At sunset, deliberately choose 5600K to preserve warmth. For a deliberately cool mood, go to 7000K+.

terms.definition: Wide shot showing the subject in its environment. Establishes the location and the relationship between subject and surroundings. The first step in coverage.
